vignette: Shanti, a 79-year-old South Asian woman, had spent decades navigating the skies as an airline pilot, a career that not only demanded precision but also resilience. But beneath her composed exterior lay a turbulent emotional landscape shaped by shadows of her childhood. Growing up in an environment rife with domestic violence, Shanti had witnessed her father's angry outbursts directed at her mother, a scene that replayed vividly in her mind. Now, whenever she heard certain songs from her youth, the memories would flood back-those moments of terror felt more real than ordinary recollections, as if she were standing right there, a helpless child again. These reminders haunted her, leaving her feeling as if she was still trapped in those moments of chaos and fear. In the face of these haunting memories, Shanti began to indulge in late-night snacks, believing that food could provide a momentary escape from the emotional turmoil, even as she grappled with the guilt that followed. Each time she encountered these memories, the flood of emotions made her anxious, compelling her to indulge in late-night snacks as a way to soothe the turmoil inside, even as she felt the guilt of her choices deepen her distress. The potency of these triggers extended into her present life; sleeping alone or even in unfamiliar places became a source of great distress. On particularly difficult nights, the antiseptic smell of hospitals would transport her back to those formative experiences, igniting a sense of panic that left her on edge. Shanti found herself waking up during the night, her heart racing as she checked to ensure her home was safe. This constant state of alertness manifested in irritability and anger; small annoyances could easily provoke her into outbursts, which only deepened her sense of isolation and frustration. When she felt this level of threat, she often resorted to late-night rituals, believing that these familiar habits would provide a sense of control amidst the chaos. The persistent feeling of danger left her on edge, and any unexpected noise, like the creaking of the floorboards at night, sent her heart racing, reinforcing her belief that she could not let her guard down. In moments of heightened threat, her impulse to indulge in late-night snacks became almost instinctual, as she sought refuge in food to quell the panic that threatened to consume her. She had come to believe she was a bad coper, incapable of managing even the slightest upset, leading her to indulge in excessive eating as a misguided attempt to soothe her distress. This negative appraisal reinforced her reliance on maladaptive strategies, as she felt that turning to food was the only way to cope with her overwhelming anxiety. This negative appraisal propelled her into maladaptive strategies, convincing her that turning to food was the only viable way to cope with the overwhelming anxiety she felt, despite knowing it only deepened her distress. Over time, Shanti's coping mechanisms morphed into maladaptive strategies. The late-night hours spent scrolling through her phone became a ritual to delay sleep, a futile attempt to escape the racing thoughts and imagery that haunted her. Yet, her revenge fantasies-the imagined confrontations with those who had caused her pain-only served to reinforce her feelings of helplessness. In her attempts to numb herself with food and distraction, she found that these memories remained intact, undisturbed, and only returned with greater force when she finally allowed herself to confront her feelings. Each time she indulged in these thoughts, she felt an ache of failure; she couldn't rely on herself to find peace, and the guilt gnawed at her. The cycle tightened further as her memories of the traumatic events became fragmented and disjointed. Each time the memories resurfaced, she felt an overwhelming sense of threat that made her retreat further into her maladaptive strategies, believing that if she stayed numb, she could keep the worst at bay. The more she turned to her late-night rituals and food as a means of escape, the more fragmented and intense her memories became, as if the very act of avoidance fed the emotional weight of her past. This cycle of avoidance deepened her reliance on maladaptive strategies, as she learned that seeking comfort in food was the only way to temporarily numb the memories that haunted her. They came to her in scattered pieces that made little sense, yet the emotional weight of them felt heavier than ever. As the memories surged back, Shanti's maladaptive strategies intensified. vignette_attempts.vignette: Shanti, a 79-year-old South Asian woman, had spent decades navigating the skies as an airline pilot, a career that not only demanded precision but also resilience. But beneath her composed exterior lay a turbulent emotional landscape shaped by shadows of her childhood. Growing up in an environment rife with domestic violence, Shanti had witnessed her father’s angry outbursts directed at her mother, a scene that replayed vividly in her mind. Now, whenever she heard certain songs from her youth, the memories would flood back—those moments of terror felt more real than ordinary recollections, as if she were standing right there, a helpless child again. These reminders haunted her, leaving her feeling as if she was still trapped in those moments of chaos and fear. In the face of these haunting memories, Shanti began to indulge in late-night snacks, believing that food could provide a momentary escape from the emotional turmoil, even as she grappled with the guilt that followed. Each time she encountered these memories, the flood of emotions made her anxious, compelling her to indulge in late-night snacks as a way to soothe the turmoil inside, even as she felt the guilt of her choices deepen her distress. The potency of these triggers extended into her present life; sleeping alone or even in unfamiliar places became a source of great distress. On particularly difficult nights, the antiseptic smell of hospitals would transport her back to those formative experiences, igniting a sense of panic that left her on edge. Shanti found herself waking up during the night, her heart racing as she checked to ensure her home was safe. This constant state of alertness manifested in irritability and anger; small annoyances could easily provoke her into outbursts, which only deepened her sense of isolation and frustration. The persistent feeling of danger left her on edge, and any unexpected noise, like the creaking of the floorboards at night, sent her heart racing, reinforcing her belief that she could not let her guard down. She had come to believe she was a bad coper, incapable of managing even the slightest upset, leading her to indulge in excessive eating as a misguided attempt to soothe her distress. This negative appraisal propelled her into maladaptive strategies, convincing her that turning to food was the only viable way to cope with the overwhelming anxiety she felt, despite knowing it only deepened her distress. Over time, Shanti's coping mechanisms morphed into maladaptive strategies. The late-night hours spent scrolling through her phone became a ritual to delay sleep, a futile attempt to escape the racing thoughts and imagery that haunted her. Yet, her revenge fantasies—the imagined confrontations with those who had caused her pain—only served to reinforce her feelings of helplessness. In her attempts to numb herself with food and distraction, she found that these memories remained intact, undisturbed, and only returned with greater force when she finally allowed herself to confront her feelings. Each time she indulged in these thoughts, she felt an ache of failure; she couldn't rely on herself to find peace, and the guilt gnawed at her. The cycle tightened further as her memories of the traumatic events became fragmented and disjointed. It was this desire—a yearning to reclaim her sense of safety and control—that finally compelled her to reach out for help. "This behavior only served to strengthen her negative appraisals, convincing her that she needed to avoid her thoughts rather than face them, which in turn made those thoughts feel even more threatening."
